clue.text: Tell, for example, has lots of money-thejammy thing!

parts.note: William Tell, the legendary crossbowman, is the best-known Swiss hero
a roll is a thick wad of banknotes

explanation.surface: A cheer for William Tell, who has come into a fortune and is a lucky fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jammy' in British slang means lucky, which is the surface sense; here it is literal: a sponge rolled up round a jam filling.
explanation.definitionFit: This rolled sponge cake is spread with jam before rolling, so it is literally a jam-filled treat.

clue.text: Injury from wind in the past

definitions.meaning: a cut or gash in the body
the past tense of wind, as in winding a clock

explanation.surface: Someone hurt in a gale long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is an injury, and the same letters form the past tense of the verb to wind.

clue.text: Established outbuilding

definitions.meaning: a building where horses are kept

explanation.definitionFit: Something steady is firmly established, and a horse's shed is a classic farm outbuilding.

clue.text: Bandit-horseman captures one

indicators.note: the horseman holds the other piece inside himself, as a captor holds a prisoner

parts.note: a horseman is a rider
A is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: A mounted outlaw seizes a victim.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandit is a robber who attacks and plunders, the same as a marauder making a raid.

clue.text: Some relief with lease expired

parts.note: to lease a property is to let it
when time has expired it is up

explanation.surface: A tenant feels a little relieved now the lease has run out.
explanation.definitionFit: A pause or slackening in pressure gives a measure of relief.

clue.text: Mutinous bosun in tirade perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters given are one possible arrangement, to be reworked

explanation.surface: A boatswain ranting at the crew might be on the verge of mutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A disobedient person defies authority, which is what a mutinous sailor does.

clue.text: Hunt for one of the brother hood?

definitions.text: Hunt for one of the brother hood?

parts.words: Hunt for one of the brother hood?
parts.note: reads like a search for a member of a gang, but Hunt is the painter William Holman Hunt, a founder of a Victorian artistic brotherhood

explanation.surface: A manhunt for a member of a criminal brotherhood.
explanation.walkthrough: William Holman Hunt co-founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of painters in 1848 with Rossetti and Millais.
explanation.definitionFit: Holman Hunt was a founding member of the 1848 brotherhood of English painters, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Care unit empty and abandoned it can be blown up

indicators.note: abandoned suggests wild, unrestrained behaviour, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: An empty care unit left abandoned might be blown up by demolition crews.
explanation.definitionFit: An air-filled wheel covering is inflated with a pump, which is what blown up means here.

clue.text: Number of shots from Norwich City, for example?

definitions.meaning: a simultaneous firing of all the guns on one side of a warship
Norwich City football team comes from the area of the Norfolk Broads, so it is a Broads side

explanation.surface: Counting the shots on goal from a Norwich City match.
explanation.walkthrough: The Norfolk Broads are waterways around Norwich, an English city; its football club is thus a 'Broads side', a team from the Broads.
explanation.definitionFit: A warship's full volley from one side is a great number of shots fired at once; the second sense is a team from the Broads.

clue.text: Religion of Simon, this, by con version

indicators.note: conversion, split so it looks like a swindler's account, means the letters are converted into a new form

explanation.surface: A man named Simon has been converted to a new religion.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the traditional faith of Japan, based on reverence for spirits of nature and ancestors.

clue.text: Full skirt

definitions.meaning: plump or complete, as in a ... figure or a ... dozen
to skirt something is to go about its edge

explanation.surface: A dressmaker describing an ample skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A plump figure is rounded or full, and to go about the edge of something is to skirt it.

clue.text: Settlebranch post

definitions.meaning: a bird may alight and settle
an old measure of length, also a pole

explanation.definitionFit: A bird alights and settles on its roost, often a branch; the word is also an old length measure and a rod or pole.

clue.text: E.g. imperial poet takes in English

indicators.note: the poet absorbs the letter inside himself

parts.note: a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: An imperial poet admits English to his work.
explanation.walkthrough: An imperial is a small pointed tuft of hair below the lower lip, named after Napoleon III.
explanation.definitionFit: An imperial is a style of facial hair, a pointed tuft on the chin.

clue.text: Carried and delivered to the orient

parts.note: a baby delivered has been born
the Orient is the East, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: Goods carried and delivered to the Far East.
explanation.definitionFit: Something carried has been borne, the past participle of to bear.

clue.text: A room for pigeons on high

parts.note: a pigeon loft is a room where pigeons are kept

explanation.surface: A room for pigeons up high in the rafters.
explanation.definitionFit: Up in the air, far above the ground, is high up.

clue.text: Nobody's daily account

parts.note: a day-by-day record kept by a nobody, recalling the comic novel by George and Weedon Grossmith about Charles Pooter

explanation.surface: An account of each day that belongs to nobody at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grossmiths' 1892 comic novel takes the form of the journal of Mr Pooter, a self-important London clerk.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily written record of events is a journal; the novel's title names one kept by a Nobody.

clue.text: This butterfly landed on the moon

definitions.meaning: a large white mountain butterfly with red eyespots
the NASA programme whose ... 11 mission put men on the Moon

explanation.surface: A butterfly that touched down on the lunar surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a mountain butterfly species and to the US space programme that put astronauts on the Moon.

clue.text: Yoke animals to vehicle, wearing cover

parts.note: to be in clothes is to be wearing them
to span is to cover or extend across

explanation.surface: Harnessing oxen to a wagon while wearing a protective cover.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a South African word from Dutch for harnessing draught animals to a wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: A South African term for harnessing oxen or horses to a wagon.

clue.text: Girl turning over hoard

indicators.note: turning over the hoard means sifting through it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl rummaging through a stash of treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so an example of a girl.

clue.text: Cheerless study to bring tears toone'seyes

parts.note: cheerless means sad
a den is a private room or study

explanation.surface: A gloomy study is enough to make anyone weep.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone unhappy is to grieve them, enough to bring tears.

clue.text: Friction at job centre some liberties taken in bar

parts.note: rubbing produces friction

indicators.note: the centre of the word job is its middle letter

explanation.surface: Friction at the job centre as liberties are taken in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, but it is a bar of music: this term means freedom in tempo within a phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, the performer speeds up and slows down for expression, taking liberties with strict time within a bar.

clue.text: Competition coming in?

definitions.meaning: an item submitted in a contest, collectively the field of contestants
the act of entering a place

explanation.surface: A contest that people are keen to join.
explanation.definitionFit: A submission to a contest, or the act of going through a door into a room.

clue.text: Why this engineering apprentice fails to get a grip?

definitions.text: Why this engineering apprentice fails to get a grip?

parts.words: Why this engineering apprentice fails to get a grip?
parts.note: without a workshop vice, a trainee cannot grip anything

explanation.surface: A trainee engineer who cannot get to grips with the job.
explanation.walkthrough: A vice is the bench clamp that holds work steady; an apprentice with 'no vice' cannot get a grip.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice is a beginner or learner, and the word split in two says he has no clamp.

clue.text: One's grandsire is one almost identical to another

definitions.meaning: Grandsire is a method in English change ringing of church bells, so a bell-puller rings it

explanation.surface: Someone who is the spitting image of their grandfather.
explanation.walkthrough: Grandsire is a traditional method in change ringing, the English art of ringing church bells in sequences.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell-puller performs a grandsire, and a lookalike is a dead double of someone.

clue.text: Blue material excavated back to front

indicators.note: back to front tells the solver to read the dug-up word in the reverse direction

parts.note: excavated means mined, dug out

explanation.surface: Some blue fabric dug up with its back where the front should be.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeans are made of this blue cotton twill fabric.

clue.text: Blockhead to waste time getting round head of Repton

indicators.note: the idling word wraps itself around the other letter

parts.note: to moon about is to waste time idly

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A dunce at Repton, a public school, keeps idling round the headmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: Repton is an English public (fee-paying) school, and 'head' suggests its headmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A blockhead is a stupid person, a fool or idiot.

clue.text: Flogs, we hear, in dungeons

indicators.note: we hear means the word is said out loud and sounds like another

parts.note: to flog goods is to sell them, so flogs means sells

explanation.surface: Prisoners are whipped down in the dungeons, so we are told.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flogs' suggests whipping, but in British slang it means sells.
explanation.definitionFit: Dungeons are prison chambers, the small rooms in which inmates are locked.

clue.text: Skill of the few caught outside

indicators.note: the abbreviation for caught sits on the outside of the other piece

parts.note: ct is a cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the Few were the RAF pilots of the Battle of Britain, after Churchill's speech

explanation.surface: The skill of the Few, Britain's wartime pilots, caught on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: Churchill called the Battle of Britain's RAF pilots 'the Few': 'never was so much owed by so many to so few'.
explanation.definitionFit: Skill is expertise, as in a trade or art requiring practised hands.

clue.text: 4's first members vehement about parting carelessly

indicators.note: the vehement word goes round the other letters

parts.note: stormy means vehement, violent

indicators.note: carelessly means done haphazardly, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: The leading raiders vehemently go about parting from one another carelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 4 is RAIDER, so '4's first members' are the first raiders in: the troops who lead an assault.
explanation.definitionFit: The troops who lead an assault on a fortress are the raiders who go in first.

clue.text: Make hole, you say? Green at it in need of repair

indicators.note: something in need of repair is broken, so these letters are fixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asking a greenkeeper to make a hole on a green in need of repair.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is spoken: 'hole' sounds like 'whole', and to make whole is to unite parts into one.
explanation.definitionFit: To combine separate parts into a unified whole, which said out loud sounds like 'make hole'.
